common_name: Ruby Cascade Peperomia (Trailing Red-Stemmed Bead Peperomia)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging container; Ruby Cascade cannot survive frost. In zone 9, grow in a container that can be moved indoors when temperatures drop below 50°F, using a small pot since Peperomia prefers to be slightly root-bound.

directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade in a hanging basket or elevated pot where the trailing stems can cascade, avoiding direct sun, which scorches the leaves. Ruby Cascade produces small, rounded, semi-succulent green leaves with a distinctive deep ruby-red underside, carried along wine-red trailing stems that show off the color contrast as the stems drape over a pot edge or hang from a basket. The combination of green tops and red undersides gives the plant a two-toned effect that catches the eye whenever the foliage moves or is viewed from below. Like other Peperomia it stores water in its succulent leaves and stems and is prone to root rot if overwatered, so allow the top inch or two of soil to dry completely between waterings.

common_name: Rana Verde Peperomia (Trailing Round-Leaf Green Peperomia)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging container; Rana Verde cannot survive frost. In zone 9, grow in a container that can be moved indoors when temperatures drop below 50°F, using a small pot since Peperomia prefers to be slightly root-bound.

directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade in a hanging basket or elevated pot where the trailing stems can cascade, avoiding direct sun, which scorches the leaves. Rana Verde carries small, plump, rounded, glossy green leaves closely spaced along slender trailing stems, similar in overall form to the popular Ruby Cascade but entirely green rather than red-tinted, giving a cooler, more uniform color for pairing with brighter or variegated companion plants. Its dense, cascading habit fills a hanging basket or shelf edge quickly once established. Like other Peperomia it stores water in its succulent leaves and stems and is prone to root rot if overwatered, so allow the top inch or two of soil to dry completely between waterings.

common_name: Napoli Nights Peperomia (Trailing Dark Purple-Black Peperomia)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging container; Napoli Nights cannot survive frost. In zone 9, grow in a container that can be moved indoors when temperatures drop below 50°F, using a small pot since Peperomia prefers to be slightly root-bound.

directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade in a hanging basket or elevated pot where the trailing stems can cascade, avoiding direct sun, which scorches the leaves. Napoli Nights carries small, rounded, glossy leaves in a deep purple-black that reads almost as true black in low light, a dramatic, moody color unlike the greens and pinks of most other trailing peperomia cultivars, giving strong contrast when paired with pale or variegated companion plants. Its compact, cascading habit works well trailing from a small hanging pot or shelf. Like other Peperomia it stores water in its succulent leaves and stems and is prone to root rot if overwatered, so allow the top inch or two of soil to dry completely between waterings.
